a b s t r a c t
Software can significantly facilitate the management ofthe complete systematic literature review process
(SLR). However, most specialized software for use in SLR processes is designed to meet the requirements
of the health and medical sciences and software engineering, and there is a need for dedicated software
for the specific research requirements of the social sciences. Furthermore, most of the software currently
used is closed and the open source code alternatives require personnel with expertise in configuration
and setup.
We present Buhos, an application for managing the complete process of systematic literature reviews
that is web-based and developed in Ruby. It offers functionalities for supporting the process of searching
screening, data extraction and reporting. Buhos can be used locally through an in-house web server, as
well as in a distributed manner, integrated with other online services.

spans.content: 1. Introduction
Buhos responds to the need for a software tool that manages
the complete process of systematic literature reviews (SLR) of
medium to high complexity in the fields of social science and
education, fields which have their particular requirements, distinct
from those of other knowledge domains. Upon analyzing the re-
sults of the Kohl et al. review [1] on software tools that partially
or fully cover the stages of an SLR, it is observed that most of
these tools have been designed with the health and medical sci-
ences and software engineering in mind, albeit being promoted
as tools for general use. SLRs designed from the perspective of
these disciplines share characteristics that do not necessarily fill
the requirements of other fields of knowledge.
In the health and medical sciences (HMS) the Cochrane Hand-
book for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2] is predominantly
used to direct the performance of systematic reviews. Most of
its indications are related to the evaluation of clinical assays and
randomized clinical trials (RCT) as these are considered to deliver
more reliable evidence than other types ofinvestigations. The focus
on a specific type of investigation enables the establishment of a
review procedure that is relatively consistent, standardized, with
defined steps, independently of the specific research question [3].
It is common practice to screen and extract information from
thousands of articles. The process can be partially automated [4,5],
as there are clear criteria for defining research questions, such
as the well-known PICOS — participants, interventions, com-
parisons, outcomes and study design [6]. For performing quality
assessments, the Cochrane manual offers a detailed analysis of
the possible bias risks, including a domain-based tool for their
assessment [2].
The focus for conducting SLRs and meta-analysis in the ambit
of social science is fundamentally different from that of HMS. The
need exists to incorporate diverse types of investigations into the
SLR, such as observational studies and case studies, as RCTs are
infrequent. In fact, it is not possible to conduct RCTs on certain
topics for ethical reasons [3,7]. It must be taken into consideration
that observational studies cannot be evaluated in as standardized
and step-by-step a manner as are RCTs [3]. Depending on the
research question, the sources of bias must be carefully assessed in
each study, considering the latter’s specific design, and carrying out
a historical, theoretical and contextualized assessment [7,8]. Thus,
a software tool for conducting SLRs in the social sciences should be
able to record in detail the search procedures, the justification for
using moderators, the coding procedures and agreements between
independent coders, seeking the greatest possible transparency in
evaluating the quality of the studies considered [8]. Besides this,
the tool must have the capability to accept different types of infor-
mation sources, since most of the evidence is not found in journals
but in grey literature, such as conferences, theses, technical reports
and other unpublished documents [9].
Therefore, developing an SLR-supporting software tool for the
social sciences requires unifying various types of investigations,
theoretical as well as empirical, in order to reach a conclusion. The
software tool utilized must be a flexible one that enables multiple
ways of performing systematic reviews, while ensuring maximum
transparency and rigor by recording each step followed by each
evaluator, especially in discrepancy resolution [10].
The studies carried out in the software engineering (SE) envi-
ronment on user requirements for SLR support software [11,12] are
pertinent for software development geared to the social sciences,
since both disciplines pose similar challenges vis à vis SLR develop-
ment. This is because the research designs utilized are generally of
an observational and post-facto nature, and the participants’ pro-
file is usually that of experts, making it difficult to establish blind
procedures [13]. Considering the main requirements described in
the literature, Buhos incorporates several tools to facilitate com-
munication between users, which, added to its ability to handle
large numbers of documents in a robust manner, enables the per-
formance of medium- to large-scale SLRs. Besides this, metadata
and files of already finished documents can be reused to update
prior reviews. With regard to software development processes,
special attention has been given to the application’s usability, test
coverage, maintainability and documentation.

Literature reviews are investigations that seek to ‘‘describe,
summarize, evaluate, clarify, and/or integrate the content of the
primary reports’’ [14, (p107)] within a specific area of knowledge,

engineering [21,22], social sciences [7,23] and education [24].

summarize, evaluate, clarify, and/or integrate the content of the

The concept of SLR can be understood either specifically or
comprehensively. The definition of SLR adopted by the Cochrane
Collaboration, associated to the manner in which it is carried out
in the HMS, indicates that the SLR ‘‘attempts to collate all em-
pirical evidence that fits pre-specified eligibility criteria in order
to answer a specific research question. It uses explicit, systematic
methods that are selected with a view to minimizing bias, thus pro-
viding more reliable findings from which conclusions can be drawn
and decisions made’’ [2, (sec1.2.2)]. An SLR must have the follow-

for including or excluding articles; (b) an explicit, reproducible
methodology; (c) systematic search capability that attempts to
identify all studies that meet the inclusion and exclusion criteria;
(d) an assessment of the validation of the evidence contained in
the studies included through bias risk assessment, for example,
and (e) a systematic presentation and synthesis of the evidence
collected [2]. These revisions are usually associated with meta-
analysis, which applies statistical methods to summarize the re-
sults. Meta-analysis is used to synthesize the evidence presented
in the different studies incorporated into the SLR to detect effects,
estimate their magnitude and variability, and analyze the factors
that influence them [25].
From a broader perspective, an SLR is considered as a review
of the literature that is exhaustive, transparent and unbiased, de-
veloped with a clearly defined methodology, performed in a sys-
tematic manner [26]. This is what differentiates it from a narrative
review, which mixes theories and opinions and does not apply a
specific method of selection and assessment to the available infor-
mation [27]. An example ofthis mode of understanding systematic
reviews is put forward by EPPI-Centre, which explicitly points
out that the only thing that differentiates a systematic review
from one that is not systematic is that ‘‘a systematic review has
an explicit, rigorous methodology. This makes the results of the
review accountable and open to criticism and debate’’ [28, (p9)].
2.2. Stages ofa systematic review
According to the guidelines of Kitchenham & Charters [13], the
systematic review process can be divided into three major phases:
planning, conducting, and reporting. Each of these phases in turn
consists of various stages. Planning the review considers: (a) iden-
tifying the need for conducting a review, (b) commissioning of the
study to an external party, (c) specifying the research question(s),
(d) developing the protocol, and (e) evaluation of the protocol by
an external agent. Performing the review involves (a) identifying
the studies through an adequate search strategy, (b) selection of
the studies, (c) evaluating the quality of the studies, (d) extracting
information from the studies and monitoring the process, and
(e) synthesizing the information. Finally, the report involves: (a)
specifying the dissemination mechanism, (b) formatting the re-
port, and (c) evaluating the report. All these stages are considered
mandatory, except for commissioning the study, evaluating the
protocol and the evaluation of the final report.
It should be kept in mind that the review process is considered
as being iterative, thus it is possible that, for instance, the protocol
will be refined following its evaluation, or that the methods of
analysis planned will be improved once the data is obtained [13].
Snowballing is an iteration-based method for identifying pertinent
studies not yielded by database searches. There are two modalities:
(a) forward-snowballing: new documents are incorporated that
cite previously selected documents, (b) backward-snowballing:
adds documents cited in the selected documents. This method is
particularly useful when a critical mass of papers has already been
identified [29].
2.3. SLR in health and medical sciences, software engineering and
social sciences
The greatest developments in SLR have been observed in the
fields of health care and health policy. It is hoped that by the end
of the decade of the 2010s, over 200,000 SLRs will have become
available to HMS [25]. In the International Prospective Register
of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), there has been a ten-fold in-
crease in the number of SLRs between 2012 and 2017, from 63 per
month in 2012 to 800 per month in 2017 [18].
SLRs in the fields of health and medicine owe their success
to their association with evidence-based medicine (EBM), defined
as ‘‘the sensible use of the best available external evidence from
systematic research, assimilated with individual clinical expertise
to evaluate the best course of care for a patient’’ [20, (p2)] The
search for evidence can be very difficult for physicians, considering
the staggering volume of research data available on Internet. The
existence of publication bias renders it even more difficult to reach
a precise assessment of the evidence [30]; thus the critical role
of the systematic review, which evaluates the available evidence
in a systematic, reproducible manner, at the same time weighing
the risk of bias [20]. For this reason, SLRs are routinely used by
researchers to inform on health practices and policies [31].
SLRs in HMS are significantly associated with the Cochrane
Database on Systematic Reviews, which is a set of reviews and
protocols maintained by specialized groups [20]. The two basic
principles of the Cochrane Collaboration are the need for unbiased
comparison of different interventions, which is the reason for their
preference for SLR in RCTs, as well as the importance of ongoing
selection and updating of the available evidence, to arrive at the
most reliable estimators of the effects [32]. Clarity in the type of
studies, as well as in the analyses considered to be appropriate,
enables establishing a standardized procedure for performing the
SLR with step-by-step instructions, as reflected in the Cochrane
Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2].
In software engineering (SE), the introduction of SLRs in the
discipline [33,34] is considered to have occurred in 2004 due to
their central role in evidence-based software engineering (EBSE)
presented by Kitchenham et al. [35], which sought to integrate
academic research and industrial practice in order to find the
best evidence sustaining the software development. Kitchenham
proposes a procedure for conducting SLRs in software engineer-
ing [36], which was updated in 2007, applying concepts from the
social sciences [13], and in 2013, following a tertiary study of 63
SLRs in the discipline [29].
SE investigation poses specific challenges that are analogous to
those of research in the social sciences. First, in HMS it is common

information from a wide variety of different types of research [13].

serve an individual effect. Unlike studies conducted in HMS, where

experts [37].

comparison of different interventions, which is the reason for their
preference for SLR in RCTs, as well as the importance of ongoing
selection and updating of the available evidence, to arrive at the
most reliable estimators of the effects [32]. Clarity in the type of
studies, as well as in the analyses considered to be appropriate,

Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2].

their central role in evidence-based software engineering (EBSE)

academic research and industrial practice in order to find the

proposes a procedure for conducting SLRs in software engineer-

SE investigation poses specific challenges that are analogous to
those of research in the social sciences. First, in HMS it is common
to restrict an SLR to RCTs or, considering the research question,
specific designs can be pinpointed as being more appropriate. In

information from a wide variety of different types of research [13].

larger software development cycle, which makes it difficult to ob-
serve an individual effect. Unlike studies conducted in HMS, where

experts [37].

41,42]. Multiple tertiary studies have been conducted to evaluate

As for the social sciences, various challenges are posed by SLRs.
First of all, while there is already a long tradition of systematic
reviews in social science, the incorporation of quantitative tools
developed in the health environment has clashed with the more
qualitative tradition in evidence gathering, particularly in the field
of education [51]. Secondly, much of the available evidence is
based on observational designs, which required undertaking the
significant methodological effort of defining the conditions under
which unbiased results could be obtained [3]. In HMS, SLRs and
meta-analysis focus on establishing homogeneous evidence which
enables establishing each treatment’s efficacy with certainty for
wide, hopefully worldwide dissemination. In contrast, the social
sciences focus on describing the heterogeneity of populations and
situations to understand the causal processes that are the basis
of a specific intervention’s successful outcome. For example, the
representativity of a study population can be more important,
or how much information is available on confounding variables,
than the presence or absence of randomization. Besides this, there
are different reporting styles even within each discipline, adding
complexity to the task of standardizing the information to be
gathered [7].
Regarding the orientations for the performance of SLRs in the
social sciences, there are important differences in approach, de-
pending on the discipline and the institutions sponsoring the stud-
ies [3]. In the field of education, the What Works Clearinghouse, a
flagship product of the Institute of Education Sciences at the U.S.
Department of Education, strongly emphasizes quantitative anal-
ysis of RCT and quasi-experimental design, with rigorous criteria
for inclusion and exclusion [16], which brings it more in line with
the Cochrane approach. The Campbell Collaboration has focused on
the effectiveness of programs, policies and practices in the fields
of crime and justice, education, international development, and
social welfare. Notwithstanding the recognition of the importance
of RCTs, it is considered advisable to include studies with designs
having less internal but greater external validity, and to add qual-
itative studies that allow for increasing the review’s explicative
capacity [32]. Finally, EPPI-Centre has focused on social policy,
including education, health, social care, developing economies,
sports, the environment and crime. It has a broad definition of
what constitutes a review, considering aggregative approaches
that seek to summarize information from different studies, such
as meta-analyses, as well as configurative approaches involving
an interpretative process of the information that is available for
producing high-level explanations [28].
Considering the variety of existing approaches for carrying out
systematic reviews in the social sciences, it is difficult to establish
a clear indicator for demonstrating its scope. A search in Scopus of
all documents in Social Sciences containing the terms ‘‘systematic
review’’ or ‘‘meta-analysis’’ in their titles with different variations,
and excluding those classified under the category ofMedicine, lists
a total of 10,100 documents, the majority from Psychology (4,679)
followed by Business, Management and Accounting (1,754).
2.4. The role ofsoftware tools in SLR
Systematic literature review processes are difficult to execute.
They require searching for hundreds of thousands of articles and
identifying which ones are useful. This entails meticulously record-
ing a great deal of information on each document. The review
process consists of several steps — prepare the topic, search
for articles, screen studies, extract data, analyze and synthesize
the data, then report findings [4]. Each step must be performed
accurately, transparently, and recorded [13]. The selection of tools,
particularly the IT tools, requires balancing initial and maintenance
costs to achieve the necessary functionality in processes having
differing degrees and levels of complexity [52].
The most important studies on the requirements of SLR users
in reference to available computer tools are those of Al-Zubidy
et al. [12] and Marshall et al. [11]. The Al-Zubidy study [12] con-
ducted with SE practitioners, concludes that multiple require-
ments exist for SLR tools. It identifies 112, and that no tool is
actually available at this time that covers them all. After analyzing
6 tools, the study found that each one covered from 32% to 68%
of the community’s requirements. Most notable were the need for
facilitated collaboration among participants located locally as well
as in different countries, the need for reductions in researchers’
work time through automated processes, for access to a central
repository with information from past SLRs, and for integration
of the different tools. Marshall et al. [11] found that researchers
who perform SLR in the social and health sciences agree with
SE researchers on the importance of management of large-scale
SLRs and the handling of communications within the team. They
also placed special emphasis on the challenges that arise during
processes of searching, selection and screening, and quality as-
sessment. Differences are observed between social science and
health science researchers with respect to SE researchers, in that
the first require version control in SLRs and the option of format-
ting the references in the final report. In addition, social science
researchers assign greater value to the possibility of carrying out
meta-analyses, having access to safety mechanisms to maintain
data confidentiality, while text analysis tools are less of a concern.
It should be emphasized that, while SLR tools can help speed
up the process and perform actions that are extremely difficult
or impossible for humans to do, they can only assist researchers
in conducting the SLR, because human judgment is required at
all stages of the process. While proposals exist for automating
most [4,5] or the entire SLR process [53], this is only possible
with a defined procedure and standardized quality criteria, which
are proper only to HMS. More specifically, in the social sciences,
the planning phase involves a process of negotiation between the
researchers, practitioners and stakeholders, which, while possible
to facilitate with computer tools, must necessarily be carried out
by the individuals concerned [28]. In SE, however, and to a greater
extent in the social sciences [7], the need for integrating various
types of investigation for different situations implies the impos-
sibility of applying a single quality criterion, as each study must
be individually assessed on the basis of its context [8]. Finally, re-
searchers need to have confidence in the reliability of automation
mechanisms before they will accept them completely [11].
2.5. Related work

mance of systematic reviews. There are programs that, while not
designed to carry out systematic reviews, provide support for the
various stages of the process. Office automation software, such
as Microsoft Word or Excel, is useful for creating forms that can
be replied to on paper or through e-mail. Web-based systems of
forms and surveys generate forms that are simple to answer and
process. While these programs are easy to setup and do not require
much training to learn to use, they make it harder to keep a record
of the project’s progress and resolve possible conflicts between
evaluators [52].

2.6. Rationalefor Buhos development
Thus, while there are tools available for managing the sys-
tematic review process in its entirety, most are not open source
and are optimized solely for biomedical and software engineering
research. From the perspective of our experience in systematic
reviews in the fields of social science and education, a software
tool is needed that can record each step of the process, including
each researcher’s communications and decisions. It must have
a defined methodology with clear stages, one that is adaptable
to the research objectives as needed. In addition, the software
must be easy to install, be available in multiple languages, and be
possible to use both locally and online on various platforms. This
will enable the development of accurate systematic reviews in the
most efficient manner possible, within a broad range of scientific
domains.
In terms of the SLR user requirements reported in the literature
[11,12], Buhos facilitates the communication between the review
users, providing an internal messaging and comments system for
the document at each phase ofthe review process. This, in addition
to the capability for managing hundreds of references swiftly,
enables Buhos to support medium and large-scale SLRs. Special at-
tention has been given to document storage, which allows reusing
both metadata and article files between different SLRs. The security
system implemented assigns specific roles for each user within
the system and is of particular importance to social science re-
searchers. For example, it enables permission to be granted solely
for accessing the review results and not the review process or the
original documents.

detection of problems. This renders the software fully functional
at each iteration of development. Finally, Buhos includes extensive

4.1. Implementation details
The Buhos application runs on Ruby [87], an interpreted open
source software that compiles on various UNIX platforms such as
Linux, as well as on Windows and MacOS. As the framework of
the web server, library Sinatra [88] is used, a DSL for the rapid
development of web applications, which can run autonomously or
be integrated into another HTTP server, such as Apache or Nginx,
through Passenger.
An effort was generally made to look for already established
libraries to provide functionalities to the system. BibTeX ruby was
used for the import and export of BibTex [89], serrano was used
for access to Crossref [90], and i18n was used for multi-language
support [91]. An internally-developed library enables accessing the
Scopus and NCBI (PubMed) database.
The Sequel library which provides ORM functionalities as well
as an abstraction layer of SQL, is used to access the database [92].
The system has been tested on MySQL and SQLite given their
popularity and functionality. The first database (MySQL) is recom-
mended for intensive use by multiple users on a shared server,
while the second (SQLite3) is useful for immediate use of the

4.2. Evaluation ofBuhos
We have evaluated the software Buhos considering three crite-
ria. The first criterion was usability. Buhos was used in a simplified
SLR process by 5 participants who had wide experience in conduct-
ing SLR, but had no prior contact with the application. The second
criterion was the extent to which Buhos satisfied the requirements
ofSLR users in the SE field, assessed by using the method described
by Al-Zubidy et al. [12]. The third criterion was coverage of tests
and maintainability. This was evaluated by using the metrics in the
website Code Climate.
The Buhos software usability test aimed to determine whether
the participants were capable of using Buhos to conduct an SLR.
Usability requirements and problems were identified and an as-
sessment made of the software’s perceived level of usability. The
test was held with 5 individuals who were experts in using SLR,
3 of them in the field of psychology and 2 in economics. Given
the participants’ time constraints, a one-hour protocol was applied
individually, involving the performance of a complete SLR, which
included simulated journal articles. In the course of the activity, a
Think Aloud protocol was followed in which each person described
what he or she thought of the application while interacting with
it. Upon completing the task, they answered a questionnaire that
included questions on sociodemographic variables, experience in
carrying out SLR and using the System Usability Scale [98], which
is a robust usability scale having broad empirical support [99].
Since all of the participants spoke Spanish, a translation used in
a previous study was employed [100].
All of the participants successfully carried out the complete SLR
procedure with an average time of 64.6 min (SD = 19.36). Through
thematic analysis [101], 12 usability problems were identified
and 17 different suggestions were made. Three bugs were also
detected and immediately corrected following application of each
procedure. The main difficulty observed was the lack of a link
that allowed the user to go back to a previous step in different
interfaces. The SUS questionnaire yielded an average score of 86.5
(DE = 8.4). Using the adjective range scale of Bangor, Kortum &
Miller [99], this average would indicate that the software is rated
on average ‘Excellent’; the minimum score of 72.5 is equivalent to
‘Good’. A detailed description methodology and results is available
in attached dataset (DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/kjn9ggxhwz.
The process based on DISSMET methodology used by Al-Zubidy
et al. [12] was used to evaluate Buhos’ suitability vis à vis SLR
user requirements in the field of SE. A rating system of Full (1
point), Partial (0.5 points) and None (0 points) was applied to
the software tool’s coverage of 53 detailed requirements. The 53
requirements are divided into 11 consolidated groupings. Each
consolidated group score is the average of the coverage scores of
the detailed requirements making up the group. The overall cover-
age score is equivalent to the weighted mean of the consolidated
requirement scores, obtained by assigning a weight from 10 to 1,
according to the order of importance in which the original study
users ranked each requirement coverage. A conservative rating
system was used, in which Buhos was only rated as having full
coverage of a detailed requirement if it provided as many as or
more functions than the other software tools evaluated in the
original study. Evaluation of each detailed requirement is available
in attached dataset (DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/kjn9ggxhwz.
Table 2 presents summarized results of the requirements anal-
ysis for Buhos. There is full coverage in Buhos for Collaboration
Support y Data Maintenance, and high level of coverage for Trace-
ability. It should be considered that there is at least partial coverage
of requirements in all areas. Although the overall coverage score is
lower than that of StArt (68%), it is comparable to those of tools
such as SESRA (59%) and Parsifal (63%), and much higher than
those ofSluRP (48%), SLRTool (44%) and SLR-Tool (32%). Thus, while
Buhos was not designed to meet the SLR requirements in SE, it
offers a degree of requirements coverage similar to those of other
available tools.
Buhos has been developed according to the methodology of
Test-driven development (TDD), wherein the developer must build
an automated unit test in the form of assertions to define the
requirements before writing the appropriate code. This implies
that software development is iterative and goes through cycles of
testing, development and refactoring [102]. Evidence exists that
the code produced with this methodology is of better quality in
terms of fewer errors, in experimental studies [103] and in case
studies [104], although the development time window is longer
and expertise is required to achieve the desired outcomes [105].
In terms of TDD implementation, Buhos has multiple unit tests
and automated integration tests that use RSpec [106]. The software
development follows the continuous integration model, in which
automated local testing is done before committing, and testing
each commit pushed to Github on an independent server through
Travis CI (https://travis-ci.org/clbustos/buhos).
Buhos yields good indicators when its code coverage and main-
tainability metrics are analyzed. According to the information
available in Code Climate (https://codeclimate.com/github/clbust
os/buhos), Buhos’ test coverage is higher than 90%. Code Climate’s
static code analysis indicates that Buhos has Category A main-
tainability, as shown by the minimal number of duplications and
excessively long methods. There is no evidence of test coverage in
other software tools except for Parsifal, in which the set of unitary
tests shows 41% coverage.
5. Illustrative example
We offer three examples to demonstrate the capabilities of
Buhos. Firstly, the Quick User Guide included in the User Manual
(http://www.buhos.org/manual/en) is available as a tutorial enti-
tled Video 1. The complete version is in http://www.buhos.org
videos.
Secondly, a description is provided of how Buhos was used
to carry out the first literary review process using then-existing
software tools for SLR. And finally, an example of how to carry
out Backward Snowballing, automated using Watir, is provided. A
screencast of the process is available, entitled Video 2.

an automated unit test in the form of assertions to define the
requirements before writing the appropriate code. This implies
that software development is iterative and goes through cycles of
testing, development and refactoring [102]. Evidence exists that
the code produced with this methodology is of better quality in
terms of fewer errors, in experimental studies [103] and in case
studies [104], although the development time window is longer
and expertise is required to achieve the desired outcomes [105].
In terms of TDD implementation, Buhos has multiple unit tests
and automated integration tests that use RSpec [106]. The software
development follows the continuous integration model, in which
automated local testing is done before committing, and testing
each commit pushed to Github on an independent server through
Travis CI (https://travis-ci.org/clbustos/buhos).
Buhos yields good indicators when its code coverage and main-
tainability metrics are analyzed. According to the information
available in Code Climate (https://codeclimate.com/github/clbust
os/buhos), Buhos’ test coverage is higher than 90%. Code Climate’s
static code analysis indicates that Buhos has Category A main-
tainability, as shown by the minimal number of duplications and
excessively long methods. There is no evidence of test coverage in
other software tools except for Parsifal, in which the set of unitary
tests shows 41% coverage.
5. Illustrative example
We offer three examples to demonstrate the capabilities of
Buhos. Firstly, the Quick User Guide included in the User Manual
(http://www.buhos.org/manual/en) is available as a tutorial enti-
tled Video 1. The complete version is in http://www.buhos.org
videos.
Secondly, a description is provided of how Buhos was used
to carry out the first literary review process using then-existing
software tools for SLR. And finally, an example of how to carry
out Backward Snowballing, automated using Watir, is provided. A
screencast of the process is available, entitled Video 2.
5.1. Revision ofSLR support software
The systematic review documented in this paper, relative to
software pertinent for developing systematic reviews, was per-
formed through Buhos. The SLR team was made up of three mem-
bers: one administrator and two analysts. The objectives of SLR
were: (1) Identify software used to perform SLR (2) Describe the
SLR software, detailing in which stages it would be used and the
objectives to be accomplished, and (3) Identify the features re-
quired for SLR software. The process began with the creation of the
systematic review, defining its objectives, inclusion and exclusion
criteria, temporal extension and approach. A personalized form
was generated consisting of two fields, one to capture information
on the names of the tools, their uses and objectives, and another
for the features required for the SLR software.
In the search stage, queries were incorporated made in different
bibliographic bases (Scopus, Ebscohost y WoS), exported to BibTeX,
as well as an informal search on Google, which was exported
from Mendeley. Each search was recorded with information on the
date, search text, description and the corresponding export file. All
searches were validated, checking that at least information about
title, year, authors and abstract were complete for each record.
In the stages that followed (titles and abstract screening, refer-
ence screening and full-text review), it was agreed by the team that
two analysts should decide on the inclusion or exclusion of each
document, based on the SLR objectives and the inclusion and ex-
clusion criteria. The administrator would need to resolve whether
each document should be included or not in the following stage.
Fig. 3 shows the evaluators’ screening interface, which allows the
analyst to include the inclusion and exclusion criteria that were
applied, and add tags and a comment to inform the administrator
of the decisions taken.
For the screening stage using title and abstract, the administra-
tor assigned to the analysts the review of the 84 documents ob-
tained from the search stage. Both analysts selected 21 documents
as useful and 56 as irrelevant; for 7 documents the result was one
vote ofapproval and another ofrejection, and these were discarded
by the administrator.
For the next stage of reference screening, all available informa-
tion must be obtained on the references cited in the included docu-
ments. Most records imported through Scopus and WoS contained
information on references, but not all; records imported through
Mendeley did not include this information. The administrator pro-
ceeded to download the information available in Crossref for each
document included in the screening stage, using the title and the
abstract, on the administration platform. 302 references contained
enough information to be incorporated as canonical documents.
27 documents were found to have two or more references in the
texts selected during the previous stage, with 9 deemed relevant
by both analysts using their titles and abstracts. These 9 documents
were added to the 21 documents previously included, for complete
review in the next stage.
In the fourth stage of full-text revision, out of the 30 documents
considered, three were excluded as they did not meet the inclusion
criteria. Specifically, the documents dealt exclusively with quan-
titative aspects of meta-analysis and not with software features
related to SLR. Prior to the work of analysis, the administrator
manually uploaded all 27 documents on PDF format and assigned
each document to a specific canonical document. It is important to
note that only the administrator and the analysts have access to the
PDFs assigned for review. If the same canonical document is used
in another review, only the metadata will be shared.
The analyst used the form created in the first stage to extract
information from the 27 included documents. As seen on Fig. 4, the
full-text revision interface shows the PDF file for the document,
the form for extracting information from the document, and the
decision interface, which is similar to the one used in the screening
stages. It should be noted that live codes can be used in the form
fields, placing the code inside brackets, later be summarized in the
reporting stage.
Finally, there are three available reports in the reporting stage.
A PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 5) is available, that can provide a
summary of the documents that were included and excluded at
each stage of the systematic review. A process report can also be
retrieved, in the form ofa web page or an Excel file, that shows all of
the analysts’ decisions and the resolutions adopted by the adminis-
trator. Both PRISMA and the process reports give an account of the
inclusion and exclusion of documents. The information extraction
report shows the information for all fields completed in full by each
analyst, and also summarizes live codes, showing how many were
used and the paragraph that each was collected from.
5.2. Backward snowballing and automation ofBuhos
One of the most important functionalities of Buhos is its capac-
ity to perform backward snowballing, i.e., to search for common
references within a set of selected documents.
To exemplify, a search was done of tertiary studies (system-
atic reviews of systematic reviews) on Software Engineering and
Global Software Engineering. A search was performed in the Sco-
pus databases (19 records), Web of Science (8 records) y IEEE (5
records) using similar search criteria. Following the deduplication
process, 24 different documents were identified, of which 21 were
accepted in the title and abstract screening. After incorporating the
references of these documents using Crossref, Buhos was able to
identify 26 documents that had been cited 2 or more times in the
documents selected during the title and abstract screening stage.
In the /spec/watir/backward_snowballing.rb route ofthe source
code the procedure previously shown is automatically replicated
using watir. The screencast is available as Video 2.
6. Conclusions
This paper presents Buhos, a web-based systematic literature
software that supplies the necessary functionalities for managing
the complete literature review process, covering the stages of
searching, screening, data extraction and reporting. The perfor-
mance of rigorous systematic summaries, developed in the most
efficient way possible, allows greater development in various sci-
entific areas, as the preceding literature is better integrated into the
new findings. The use of software allows researchers to track their
decisions and disagreements, an extremely cumbersome process
when performed manually. And because Buhos can be used in a
distributed manner in multiple languages, systematic reviews can
be carried out by multiple researchers working in conjunction from
their respective countries. This would be particularly useful in SE,
for teams developing SLR running Global Software Development.
In the case of Social Sciences, using international work teams
would avoid bias associated with language or cultural position, a
significant factor for ensuring the validity of results in this field of
knowledge [107].
During the development period, the software was integrated
in a natural manner to the workflow of various researchers, who
remarked on the improved organization oftheir work and how the
software’s capability for analyzing citation relationships between
articles greatly facilitated gaining new insights into the literature.
Specifically, the software is being used by five doctoral students of
Psychology in Chile’s University of Concepción who are simultane-
ously conducting online systematic reviews. The most advanced of
these is a systematic review on the crisis of replicability in social
psychology, coordinating the work of four reviewers.
